d.title: Hallucination rate has two definitions, and one of them is measurable
d.caption: The percentage of factual claims unsupported by **ground truth** needs somebody to establish what is true, which is as expensive as it sounds and bounds the eval set by annotation effort. The percentage unsupported by **the retrieved context** needs nothing external — the context is right there — which is why groundedness is the version that gets measured and 8.8 develops it. They are different quantities: a grounded answer can be wrong if the context was wrong.

nodes.label: Needs someone to establish truth
nodes.sub: expensive, and it caps the set

d.title: The operative instruction is 'disaggregated by group'
d.caption: Perspective API, ToxiGen, BBQ and BOLD are the standard suites, and the part that does the work is not the suite — it is reporting **disaggregated by group**. An aggregate toxicity or bias score averages over exactly the dimension the measurement exists to examine, so a model that is fine on most groups and poor on one reports as fine. Which is the same structural error as 6.5's modality aggregate: the average hides the only thing worth knowing.

nodes.label: Averages over the dimension of interest

d.title: The corpus is the one input a RAG pipeline trusts by construction
d.caption: Attack suites measure the percentage of refusals that **hold under attack**, which is the right framing: a refusal rate on benign input tells you nothing about robustness. 6.7 covered the RAG-specific case and it is the harder one — injection arriving through a retrieved document, where **the corpus is the input the pipeline was designed to trust**. So the measurement has to include adversarial documents in the index, not just adversarial queries at the boundary.

d.title: Calibration, and what a 0.20 overconfidence shift does to ECE
d.caption: Bin by stated confidence, take the absolute gap between mean confidence and actual accuracy in each bin, and average weighted by bin size. A well-calibrated model reads **ECE 0.0136** with accuracy 0.758 against mean confidence 0.749 — essentially tracking. Shift confidence up by 0.20 and ECE becomes **0.2075**, and the per-bin table shows the damage is uniform: every bin is between 0.175 and 0.245 overconfident, so this is a systematic offset rather than a failure at the extremes.

d.title: Five retrieval metrics, each answering a different question
d.caption: Stated as questions they stop being interchangeable. **Recall@k asks did we get them; Precision@k asks how much noise; MRR asks how high.** Hit rate asks only whether anything relevant arrived, which is the weakest and the one module 5 used throughout. nDCG weights by rank and normalises against the ideal ordering, which makes it the only one that grades the *whole* ordering rather than a cut of it.
cells: fraction with at least one relevant
mean of 1/rank of the first hit

d.title: Three of these need no gold answer, which is what lifts the ceiling
d.caption: 8.1 argued that reference-free evaluation is what removes the cap on eval-set size, because a gold answer per case bounds you by annotation effort. Here is where that pays: **faithfulness, answer relevancy and context precision all need no reference**, so they can run on every production request. Context recall and answer correctness need gold answers and therefore stay on a curated set — which is the natural division between what you measure continuously and what you measure in CI.
cells: are the claims supported by the context?
are the chunks relevant and well ranked?

d.title: Seven dimensions, because task success catches everything non-specifically
d.caption: The first row is what everyone measures and it tells you nothing about *why*. The rest decompose it. **Tool-argument correctness catches a valid call that asks the wrong question** — schema-valid and semantically wrong, which 1.8's banana at 3,000 calories is the archetype of. Trajectory quality catches the right answer reached by luck. And the last row is the one with a trap: measure cost per **resolved** task, because cost per *attempt* rewards giving up early.

d.title: Three ways to score a path, and what each one punishes
d.caption: Gold-trace matching is deterministic and cheap and **punishes valid alternative routes** — which matters because most tasks have several. Judging the trajectory handles that and imports every bias from 8.6, position and verbosity included. Outcome-only is correct when the path genuinely does not matter, and 7.9's reasoning models are the case where it does not: the model was rewarded on the answer alone and discovered its own path.

d.title: Four kinds of case, and the one worth most per example
d.caption: Happy paths are cheap to write and **the least informative per case** — they catch an obvious regression and nothing else. The highest-value cases you own are the **known past bugs**: each one is a failure you have already paid for, and a regression test on it is the only way to stop paying twice. Edge cases are where behaviour is undefined unless somebody defined it, and adversarial inputs are 6.7's case where the corpus is the attack surface.

cells.text: lowest - catches an obvious regression, nothing more

cells: boundaries, empty results, odd formats - undefined unless defined

cells.text: highest - a failure you already paid for

d.title: Gate on the metrics, and know that the right stopping point looks unremarkable
d.caption: A CI gate turns the golden set into a deployment condition rather than a report nobody reads. The caution comes from 7.15: **the right stopping point looks unremarkable when you reach it.** In the simulated alignment run the true quality peak sat at a KL of 1.0 where the held-out eval was up only slightly — so a gate tuned to demand an impressive improvement will walk straight past the optimum and keep going into the region where quality collapses.

nodes.label: So gate on 'no regression'
nodes.sub: rather than on a big win

d.title: Six classes of signal, and the free one people skip
d.caption: Explicit feedback is what teams build first and it is **rare and self-selecting** — the people who click a thumb are not a sample of your users. **Implicit feedback is free, abundant and unbiased by who bothers to click**: copy rate, follow-up edits, abandonment, regenerate clicks. A/B is the only causal measurement on the list. And drift is invisible offline **by construction**, because an offline set cannot contain a distribution it was not drawn from.

cells.text: free, abundant, unbiased by who clicks

cells: a rising rate is a signal, not just a shield

cells.text: what you are actually paid for

d.title: Measure all three axes, because a quality win usually loses two of them
d.caption: A change that improves answers by adding a re-ranking pass and a longer prompt **will win on quality and lose on both latency and cost** — and 6.2 measured the magnitude: 11 ms of retrieval against 2,405 ms of re-ranking. An A/B that reports only the quality metric therefore recommends shipping something that triples the per-request bill, and nothing in the result says so. Three axes, every time.

nodes.label: Add a re-ranker and a longer prompt
Report all three, or recommend wrongly

d.title: The no-results rate is the cheapest leading indicator in a RAG system
d.caption: It rises when queries move away from the corpus, and crucially **it rises before answer quality visibly degrades** — because the system is still producing fluent answers from whatever it did retrieve. Which makes it a leading indicator rather than a lagging one, and it costs a counter. The same logic applies to rising fallback usage: both measure *the gap between what users ask and what you indexed*, which is the thing that actually drifts.

d.title: One case, scored by every metric in the module
d.caption: The point of running every metric on a single example is that **they disagree in instructive ways**. Two chunks retrieved, one relevant; an answer that is correct and well-grounded. Recall@2 is a perfect 1.0 and Precision@2 is 0.5, from the same retrieval. Faithfulness reads 1.0 — and §03 shows that score depends on an **unwritten policy** about whether derived claims count as supported. A dashboard showing one of these numbers tells a different story from a dashboard showing another.

d.title: Six metrics on one answer, and the pair that disagree
d.caption: Every number here is defensible and they do not say the same thing. **Recall@2 is 1.0 and Precision@2 is 0.5 on the identical retrieval** — so "retrieval was good" and "retrieval was half noise" are both true, and which one you put on a dashboard is a choice about what you want to be alarmed by. Context precision is low-ish because the noise sits at rank 2, which is the metric that notices *ordering* rather than membership.

d.title: Seven tools, placed on the layer each one serves
d.caption: The tools sort cleanly onto 8.1's two jobs, and the first row exists **because** of 8.4: a standardised harness is the only way to make benchmark numbers comparable when harness settings move them by points. RAGAS implements 8.8's quartet. DeepEval and promptfoo are the CI gate of 8.10, and the tracing tools are what close 8.11's online loop — which is the layer most teams reach last and should reach first.

d.title: Seven pitfalls, and the two that this module measured as worse than stated
d.caption: Two rows are sharper than the received wisdom. **An inverted sentence scored ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 of exactly 1.0000** — so "BLEU/ROUGE don't measure correctness" understates it; they can award a perfect score to a reversal of meaning. And **a judge outputting "good" for everything got 95.1% raw agreement and κ = 0.000** — so raw agreement is not evidence of a working judge, and Cohen's κ is the number that catches it.
